text:
我大姐是公安，性子强势火爆，平日里总动辄责骂姐夫。姐夫41岁那年突发疾病离世，送医后已经抢救无效。

出事那天早上，姐夫照常早起做好早饭，我姐却不停挑毛病，嫌粥太稀、鸡蛋煎老。姐夫默默把煎蛋夹给孩子，自己喝着稀粥。

孩子夸赞爸爸煎蛋好吃，我姐立刻瞪眼嘲讽姐夫手艺差，姐夫全程沉默，吃完便拿钥匙送孩子上学。出门前他看向我姐，有话想说却最终咽了回去，我姐只顾对着镜子涂口红，完全没留意。

送完孩子，姐夫没有直接去公司，特意绕道买了我姐爱吃的草莓。他提着草莓走到小区楼下，忽然捂着胸口蹲倒，邻居见他脸色惨白急忙拨打 120。救护车赶到时，姐夫已经说不出话，手里还紧紧攥着那袋草莓。

医院来电时，我姐刚换好警服准备上班，接电话时还十分不耐烦。听到医生说人快要不行，她的警帽 “啪” 地掉在地上。她发疯似的赶往医院，路上连闯两个红灯，脑海里全是清晨姐夫望向她的眼神。

从前她总嫌弃姐夫窝囊没本事，却忘了他每天五点起床做饭，无论多晚都等她回家，她的警服永远熨得平整，爱吃的菜总摆在餐桌正中。

赶到医院时姐夫已经进了抢救室，医生出来摇头，说是急性心梗，送来太晚无力回天。我姐当场瘫坐在地上，泪水止不住地淌。

她想起前一晚姐夫说胸口发闷，想让她陪自己去检查，可她当时忙着整理案卷，只说他小题大做。这么多年，姐夫从来不和她争执，任凭她怎么数落，都只是默默忍受。

姐夫的葬礼上，孩子抱着遗像哭得撕心裂肺，不停念叨爸爸做的煎蛋最好吃。我姐站在一旁浑身发抖，听见邻居私下说姐夫是常年受气憋出的病，她无从辩驳，心里清楚大家说得没错。那天早上姐夫眼里藏着委屈、不舍，还有她当初没能看懂的绝望。

姐夫走后，我姐再也没有发过脾气。她每天五点起床做饭，学着姐夫的样子煎蛋、煮稠粥，时常洗一盘草莓摆在桌上，却再也尝不出酸甜。

看着镜子里办案时雷厉风行的自己，她才明白，自己争赢了所有口舌，却弄丢了包容她所有坏脾气的人。

后来收拾遗物，她在姐夫抽屉找到一本日记，离世当天的最后一页写着：今天想跟她说我爱她，也想告诉她，我有点累了。

看到这句话，我姐终于崩溃大哭。她终于懂了，强势算不上本事，懂得珍惜才最重要，可明白这个道理时，一切都太迟了。

孩子上小学那天，我姐牵着他走到校门口，大风吹乱了她的头发。孩子轻声说，以前爸爸也是这样牵我。

我姐蹲下来抱紧孩子，眼泪打湿了校服，心底不停地说对不起，对不起，可那个会包容她的男人，再也听不见了。。。

text:
There will be no rotation against Ecuador tomorrow. The only changes announced by Julian Nagelsmann are: Rüdiger instead of the injured Schlotterbeck, and Raum instead of Nene Brown, who's carrying muscular problems 

Nagelsmann explains his decision not to rotate: "That's the most legitimate question of all, the discussion about whether or not to make changes. We in the coaching staff also discussed and considered this extensively. Looking at the weeks leading up to the World Cup, one of the key topics was that the team needed time to gel and that we hadn't played enough games together. Now we've played two matches, and we're already debating how many changes to make. I don't see the point in that. With Kai, Jamal, and Felix, we had players who were away from the national team for up to a year. We've now secured two wins, which is important for the standings. But we still have one game left, which we want to win and use to prepare for the knockout stage. I understand every discussion about Deniz [Undav] having earned his place in the starting lineup; that's certainly true. Nevertheless, we have a reasoned approach to our decisions, and we make them with conviction. Therefore, we will make the necessary changes tomorrow, because 'Nene' (Brown) is carrying a knock and Schlotti has unfortunately suffered a serious injury. Otherwise, we will approach the game the same way we have in recent matches"

text:
国内吸毒的人群其实正在断崖式下跌，连戒毒所都快清空了，里面的管教都在分流去学心理疏导，因为根本没收容对象了。

别不信，治好这些老毒虫的不是什么道德感化，而是两个字：太穷。

现在国内对易制毒化学品的管控严格到变态，实验室买点基础试剂都得专车专人专柜。这直接导致毒品产量暴跌，价格飙升。以前冰毒一百块一克，现在两三千。

我亲戚就是个老毒虫，以前进过无数次强戒所都戒不掉。现在他彻底老实了，因为他根本吸不起。

以前靠骗父母、骗朋友还能凑合，现在他就是把全家卖了也凑不够一口的钱。在绝对的贫穷面前，什么心瘾难除、什么心理戒断困难，全都是伪命题。买不起，他就得给我老老实实当个普通人。

所以，没有什么瘾是穷治不好的。如果有，那只是因为他还不够穷。

text:
聊聊智谱市值破万亿为什么不是高估

事先声明, 个人观点仅供参考. 

直接说结论, 智谱在 GLM 的 Agent 能力训练上是有东西的. 而且是领先的.

给没看过我这个评测的同学简单介绍下, 这是个我做的使用 tool_call 模拟大模型送外卖的测试 silicon-rider-bench, 大模型要像人类骑手一样接单, 然后选择合适的订单进行配送.

这个测试我累计测了30个模型, 几乎包含了近半年的全部国产大模型.

GLM-5 至 GLM-5.2 从测试上来看能明显感觉到3个阶段的进化:

最开始 GLM-5 是在所有测试模型中第一个能做到反思自己上下文行为, 然后做出改进的. 比如大部分被测试模型发现自己送餐超时被扣钱了, 都会说下次要避免. 但是只有 GLM-5 会真的采取措施, 比如尝试少接单来提升准时率.

轮到 GLM-5.1 则是所有测试模型中, 第一个实现了送顺路单的, 它在接单前就会尝试自己思考合并送餐路线, 然后送顺路单, 直接把路径效率压缩到了比单次送餐的距离理论值还低(因为同时送了n餐).

这次 GLM-5.2 更进一步, 它只在测试开始看了一遍地图, 接下来就直接把地图记住了, 包括哪个地点附近有哪些餐厅, 甚至最猛的是电动车没电了换电的时候, 它直接就能去换电站, 而不是调用 search_nearby_battery_stations() tool_call 来搜索. 节省下来的 tool_call 全都用来实际推进任务了, 而不是用来大量获取信息. 从分数上来看直接断崖式领先了.

不要小看这个「大部分tool_call都能用来推进任务」的能力, 转换到 Agentic Coding, 意味着它理解项目的能力可能是其他模型的数倍, 消耗少量的 token 就能产出高质量的结果.

从结果来看, 这个榜单直到 kimi-k2.7-code 出现之前, 连一个能超越 GLM-5 Agent 能力的模型都没有. 要知道 GLM-5 还是 2 月份发布的.  从这点来看, 智谱的 Agent 能力训练至少领先了其他国产模型2-4个月. 即最大2个代差.

所以智谱市值破万亿从技术层面来看, 完全不是用脚投票.

#GLM52 #AIAgent

text:
马斯克在 X 上敲下了一句狠话：新加坡正在走向灭绝。

别觉得他是在口嗨。地缘经济正在大洗牌，当时代抛弃一个国家时，最先撞墙惨死的绝对不是大国，而是那些依赖单一流量生存的小而美孤岛。

第一个死穴：0.97的魔幻生育率。

新加坡的本国人口正在每25年腰斩一次。政府发再多奶粉钱也无济于事，因为这个花园城市已经把房价、教育和内卷变成了年轻人的绝望之谷。养娃几十万起步，还得赡养长寿的父母。既然活得像个耗子，年轻人干脆选择躺平：对不起，我是最后一代。
为了自救，新加坡疯狂搞自动化。可机器人不买房，不交公积金，更没有国家认同。这里越来越像一个高级、高网速的“全球共享办公室”。所有人都在这赚钱，但没有一个人把它当家。
第二个死穴：马六甲海峡的垄断神话破灭。

以前新加坡靠当中间商躺赚，但现在全球供应链正在疯狂去新加坡化。周边国家的大型深水港、自贸区和零关税政策正在降维打击，海南封关更是釜底抽薪。
货轮数量暴跌，资金、高管和跨国金融机构开始成批北移。在那个追求效率的旧时代，中间商赚差价；但在今天这个安全优先、大国博弈的碎片化时代，中间商往往最先被踢出局。
未来的生存大逃杀极其残酷。

真正的赢家，是那些既有庞大产业链，又能实现人口自我刷新的大陆型巨头。
新加坡的悲剧在于，它把旧时代的中间商剧本演到了极致和完美，却发现新时代直接换了游戏。一旦资金流和货运流绕开你，那些闪闪发光的 CBD 摩天大楼，就不再代表未来，它们只是时代车轮碾过去后，留下一座高造价的旧纪念碑。
#地缘政治 #马斯克 #新加坡 #人口危机 #全球经济 #供应链

中国这一波中上游985，也包括大部分C9，包括南开大学、天津大学、吉林大学、山东大学、东南大学，

电子信息计算机专业大一到大三，辅导员是要抓晚自习、查寝和月考的，完全是他妈衡水中学的管理水平。

因为我说过，清华50%的教授是傻逼，下面学校教授90%是傻逼，根本不好好上课， 结果就是上课内容非常无聊，学生根本不想听课，但学生都是好学生、优质做题家，至少考前冲击刷个GPA还是没问题的。

结果就是大一大二刷题刷GPA，上晚自习查寝，大三大四准备考研考公考编，这种中游985大部分人刷题是没问题的，但是基本什么行业经验和能力都没锻炼出来，大学四年手写代码总量不到1万行的大有人在。

这种学校就是往死里毁孩子，唯一KPI就是往上考清华上交浙大，剩下的孩子本校保研大锅端，再剩下的孩子考公或者二战考研，等于把孩子们本科四年宝贵时间全浪费了。

这种培养方式，是远远不如深职院这种轰着你实习、做项目、打比赛的培养模式的。

text:
Anthropic 今天正式致信美国参议院银行委员会和白宫，指控阿里巴巴旗下的通义千问（Qwen）AI 实验室对 Claude 发动了迄今为止规模最大的蒸馏攻击。

根据 CNBC 和 Reuters 获取的信件内容，通义千问关联方在 4 月 22 日到 6 月 5 日期间，通过大约 25,000 个虚假账号与 Claude 进行了超过 2880 万次交互。攻击的目标很明确：Claude 最核心的软件工程和 Agent 推理能力。

这个数字放到上下文里才知道有多夸张。今年 2 月，Anthropic 公开点名过 DeepSeek、MiniMax 和 Moonshot AI 三家，说它们用大约 24,000 个假账号总共产生了 1600 万次交互。阿里巴巴一家的量，接近之前三家加起来的两倍。

所谓蒸馏攻击（adversarial distillation），简单说就是拿别人家的顶级模型当老师，大规模喂它问题，收集回答，再用这些回答训练自己的模型。这样做的好处是可以跳过数百万甚至数十亿美元的独立研发成本，快速接近对手的能力水平。Claude 在中国是不可用的，所以这些操作本身就违反了 Anthropic 的服务条款和地域限制。

Anthropic 在信中写道，这些蒸馏攻击是系统性的、工业化规模的，目的是收割美国 AI 能力，然后重新包装成自己的产品。阿里巴巴对此未予置评。

这件事的时机很微妙。Anthropic 现在跟特朗普政府的关系并不好。就在 6 月 12 日，商务部以国家安全为由下令 Anthropic 停止向所有外国人提供其最新的 Fable 5 和 Mythos 5 模型的访问权限，包括 Anthropic 自己的外籍员工。Anthropic 不得不在全球范围内关闭这两个模型，到现在还没恢复。Anthropic 公开表示不同意这一决定，认为一个"狭窄的潜在越狱漏洞"不应该成为召回已部署给数亿用户的商业模型的理由。

所以 Anthropic 现在的处境相当拧巴：一边在跟华盛顿说中国公司在偷我们的技术，请帮忙，一边在跟同一个政府争论你不该限制我们的模型。

不过国会两党在这件事上倒是有共识。参议员 Bill Hagerty（共和党）和 Andy Kim（民主党）计划在必须通过的国防授权法案中提出修正案，对被发现非法获取美国 AI 模型输出的中国公司实施制裁或列入黑名单。Anthropic、OpenAI 和 Google 三家也已经联合起来，共享蒸馏攻击的情报信息。

Anthropic 目前估值 9650 亿美元，本月已秘密提交了 IPO 申请，最早可能今年秋天上市。蒸馏攻击对一家即将上市的公司来说是实打实的商业威胁，中国竞争对手用极低的成本复制出接近的产品，直接侵蚀市场空间。

result.text:
Anthropic 今天正式致信美国参议院银行委员会和白宫，指控阿里巴巴旗下的通义千问（Qwen）AI 实验室对 Claude 发动了迄今为止规模最大的蒸馏攻击。

根据 CNBC 和 Reuters 获取的信件内容，通义千问关联方在 4 月 22 日到 6 月 5 日期间，通过大约 25,000 个虚假账号与 Claude 进行了超过 2880 万次交互。攻击的目标很明确：Claude 最核心的软件工程和 Agent 推理能力。

这个数字放到上下文里才知道有多夸张。今年 2 月，Anthropic 公开点名过 DeepSeek、MiniMax 和 Moonshot AI 三家，说它们用大约 24,000 个假账号总共产生了 1600 万次交互。阿里巴巴一家的量，接近之前三家加起来的两倍。

所谓蒸馏攻击（adversarial distillation），简单说就是拿别人家的顶级模型当老师，大规模喂它问题，收集回答，再用这些回答训练自己的模型。这样做的好处是可以跳过数百万甚至数十亿美元的独立研发成本，快速接近对手的能力水平。Claude 在中国是不可用的，所以这些操作本身就违反了 Anthropic 的服务条款和地域限制。

Anthropic 在信中写道，这些蒸馏攻击是系统性的、工业化规模的，目的是收割美国 AI 能力，然后重新包装成自己的产品。阿里巴巴对此未予置评。

这件事的时机很微妙。Anthropic 现在跟特朗普政府的关系并不好。就在 6 月 12 日，商务部以国家安全为由下令 Anthropic 停止向所有外国人提供其最新的 Fable 5 和 Mythos 5 模型的访问权限，包括 Anthropic 自己的外籍员工。Anthropic 不得不在全球范围内关闭这两个模型，到现在还没恢复。Anthropic 公开表示不同意这一决定，认为一个"狭窄的潜在越狱漏洞"不应该成为召回已部署给数亿用户的商业模型的理由。

所以 Anthropic 现在的处境相当拧巴：一边在跟华盛顿说中国公司在偷我们的技术，请帮忙，一边在跟同一个政府争论你不该限制我们的模型。

不过国会两党在这件事上倒是有共识。参议员 Bill Hagerty（共和党）和 Andy Kim（民主党）计划在必须通过的国防授权法案中提出修正案，对被发现非法获取美国 AI 模型输出的中国公司实施制裁或列入黑名单。Anthropic、OpenAI 和 Google 三家也已经联合起来，共享蒸馏攻击的情报信息。

Anthropic 目前估值 9650 亿美元，本月已秘密提交了 IPO 申请，最早可能今年秋天上市。蒸馏攻击对一家即将上市的公司来说是实打实的商业威胁，中国竞争对手用极低的成本复制出接近的产品，直接侵蚀市场空间。

text:
看完《置身米内》后的一点感触。

判断一家公司对员工好不好，最简单的标准就是看打卡。

最好的企业，比如外企，根本不打卡。

差一点的，比如腾讯，一天打一次卡。

再差一点的，比如美团，一天凑够 8 小时就行，系统上还会清清楚楚地显示你几点打的卡。

到了小米这里，事情变得非常拧巴。

第一，办公软件上根本不显示你的上下班打卡时间。你得自己猜几点打的卡，甚至要猜哪台机器才算数。这种不确定性本身就是手段，目的就是让你心里没底，主动多留一会儿，自愿加班。

第二，从去年开始，要求员工日均工时不低于 11.5 小时。这事当时在内部掀起了不小的风波。

最岳不群的地方在于，这些要求全靠口头传达，不留任何书面痕迹。一套岳不群式的做法，查无实据，体面照旧。

我所有去了小米的朋友，吐槽的第一件事都是工资低，远不如华为和主流互联网厂。

小米招人的核心标准就是"高性价比"，本质上它根本不算一家互联网公司。

以上这些，和它对外宣传的那个伟光正形象，差得太远了。

text:
AI 行业有个正在被验证的规律：真正模型做得好的，不是大厂，是专门做 AI 的公司。

Anthropic 全部身家就押在 AI 上，100% 的人和钱砸在模型和 Agent 上。OpenAI 也是，连 Sora 都砍了集中资源做 Codex。这两家飞轮转得最快，营收增长也最猛。

Google 呢？主营是搜索、GCP、YouTube 广告，加起来每年几千亿美元。AI 在里面占比还很小。AI 战略得服从整体营收大盘，没法 all-in。

国内其实也一样——跑在前面的是 DeepSeek、智谱、Kimi 这些专做模型的公司，不是腾讯混元、阿里千问、字节豆包。大厂的 AI 业务线营收占比太小，战略上就是跑不快。

说白了，往已有产品里"加 AI"和从零做 AI 原生产品，是两条完全不同的路。大厂擅长前者，但后者才是这个时代真正的命脉。这是结构性的问题，不是换个领导就能解决的。详细分析录了一期。

text:
这事儿为什么让人感觉恶心？

因为这根本不是什么所谓的江湖情义，而是顶级资本对底层普通民众最傲慢的情感勒索。

那些动辄坐拥几十亿身家、出入前呼后拥、手上掌握着顶级社会资源的大导演和大明星，在需要普通人掏真金白银买单的时候，突然摘下名表，换上黑T恤，开始跟台下每个月为几千块碎银几两拼尽全力的打工人称兄道弟、要起了面子。

商业电影本是一场“一手交钱，一手交戏”的对等消费。电影好，观众自然买账；电影烂，观众退场是应当应分。

可有些高高在上的精英偏不，他们要把商业失败的风险，用一句话轻轻巧巧地转变成观众“不讲义气”、“不给面儿。”

冯小刚们日进斗金、在豪宅里指点江山的时候，谁跟普通老百姓讲过面儿？

普通人为了生计苦苦挣扎、被生活毒打得鼻青脸肿的时候，又有哪个手握特权的人，俯下身来给老百姓“走个面”？

收起那套“爷们姐们儿”的江湖做派吧。普罗大众没有义务去用自己送外卖的血汗钱，给这些富豪们的面子添砖加瓦。

有本事就拍好电影，让大家伙儿心甘情愿地掏钱买票。

text:
穷人和富人最大的差距，藏在那些看不见的摩擦成本里。

前几天看到一个视频，一个穷人家出身的女生第一次住高级酒店，突然发现富人的生活几乎没有摩擦：洗衣、洗鞋有人代劳，健身房、泳池就在楼下。同样是想锻炼、想游泳，富人的决策成本极低，因为这些服务本来就摆在那里，伸手就能用。

我从小见过太多相反的场景。我爸妈一辈子都在省电费、省空调费、省交通费。

最典型的是省交通，明明打车十分钟到的地方，穷的时候你就得走四十分钟，或者挤三十分钟公交。

通勤这件事我感触特别深。在北京待久了就知道，去任何一个地方坐公交地铁基本不会低于一个小时。

算上上班和周末，一个只能坐公共交通的人，每天都有大把时间被通勤吃掉。

但富人可以花钱买回这些时间。每次出门打专车，省下半小时不说，安静的车厢里还能打电话、开线上会议，把这半小时直接变成生产时间。对时间值钱的人来说，这笔账怎么算都划算。

所以随着时薪的提升，我开始有意识地模仿这种习惯，也就是给自己的时间标个价。如果你一小时能挣300，那花 70打车省下一小时，没什么好犹豫的。

我的时薪从100到 500再到1000，越往后越果断地用钱换时间：能打车绝不挤公交；累了就近开个钟点房补觉。

这些其实都是把自己当成一门生意来经营——用的是做生意赚钱的模式，不是省钱过日子的模式。

text:
$META 是美国最没出息的科技公司

Meta就像腾讯一样，抄袭文化深入骨髓

Meta的所有产品都是抄来的

公司最早叫Facebook。Facebook就是创始人小扎抄袭温克沃斯兄弟的产品

后来Facebook变成了电子坟场，小扎马上“拿来主义”买了instagram和whatsapp。这三者和Facebook一起，都成了全球电信诈骗广告的温床。电诈广告收入，是小扎公司的重要收入来源

text:
浙江宁波一男子，因为前年结婚时被邻居收了两千块过路费，昨天邻居儿子娶媳妇，他把自家三轮车横在了巷子口，车身前放了块大纸板，写着喜事通行吉祥如意，下面补了行小字建议金额两千元。
 
巷子不宽，三轮车一横，婚车根本过不去。邻居家的喜娘急得直跺脚，扯着嗓子喊：“老张！你这是干啥？
大喜的日子别添堵！”男子蹲在车斗上抽烟，眼皮都没抬：“我这不写着吉祥如意吗？跟你家当年对我做的一样。”
 
围观的人越聚越多，有老人劝：“都是街坊，低头不见抬头见，算了吧。”男子弹了弹烟灰，指着巷尾的老槐树：“前年我娶媳妇，就从这树底下过，他爹拦着不让走，说‘过我家门口，得讨个彩头’，两千块少一分都不让进。我妈给我打电话时，新娘子在婚车里坐了快一小时，红盖头都哭湿了。”
 
邻居家的老头挤进来，脸涨得通红：“那不是图个吉利吗？谁让你家车队那么气派，我以为你不差这钱。”

男子笑了，从车斗里翻出个红本本，是当年的收条，上面还歪歪扭扭写着“喜钱两千，概不退还”。“我家那车是租的，为了撑场面借了三万块，这两千块还是我媳妇陪嫁里拿的。”
 
婚车司机按喇叭催，新郎官穿着西装跑过来，往男子手里塞烟：“张叔，您高抬贵手，今天是我大喜的日子，有啥恩怨咱过后说。”男子没接烟，指了指纸板：“我也不难为你，按上面写的来，一分不多要，一分不能少。”
 
新娘的娘家亲戚不乐意了，吵着要报警。

男子掏出手机：“报吧，让警察评评理，当年他爹收我过路费的时候，算不算敲诈。”这话一出，邻居家的人顿时没了声，谁都知道，那年头收“过路费”本就不合规矩，不过是仗着老张是外来户，好欺负。
 
僵持了半小时，村里的老支书来了，把两人拉到一边说：“老张，他爹当年做得不对，我替他给你赔个不是。但今天是孩子的好日子，别让喜事变了味。”转头又对邻居老头说：“你把当年的钱还了，再道个歉，这事就算了。”
 
老头磨磨蹭蹭从口袋里摸出两千块，往老张手里一塞，嘟囔着：“算我倒霉。”

老张接过来，数都没数，转身递给旁边的新郎：“这钱你拿着，给你媳妇买束花。”然后把三轮车挪到路边，拍了拍车座：“我不是要这钱，是要个理。谁都别觉得外来户好欺负，规矩面前，人人一样。”
 
婚车缓缓开过巷子时，新娘从车窗里探出头，给老张鞠了一躬。围观的人都说老张做得对，“当年那事确实过分，换谁都咽不下这口气”。老张收拾纸板的时候，阳光照在他黝黑的脸上，他突然笑了，原来讨公道不一定得红着眼吵架，有时候，把对方做过的事原原本本还回去，比啥都有力量。
 
下午路过老张家门口，见他正在修三轮车，车斗里放着刚买的菜。邻居家的喜宴鞭炮声传来，他抬头望了望，嘴角翘了翘，继续手里的活。有些恩怨，不是要记一辈子，是要让对方知道，尊重这东西，你不给别人，自己也得不到。

2019年10月29日，以色列海法举办了一场“和平慈善赛”。由巴西传奇队对阵以色列明星队。

当时卡卡在中圈附近带球推进，以色列女裁判突然吹停比赛，并在卡卡一脸茫然时向他出示了一张黄牌。

随后，女裁判微笑着掏出手机，卡卡这才反应过来对方是为了“公器私用”追星自拍，随即大方配合合影。

最终巴西传奇队以 4:2 战胜了以色列明星队，卡卡在比赛中还贡献了一记精彩的进球。

text:
本地用vLLM部署GLM-5.2的速度终于上来了! 

好消息终于轮到本地部署 GLM-5.2 了! 大家都知道 GLM-5.2 这次是自带了MTP头的, 可以进行推测性解码. 

但是, 这个只适用于bf16原始精度的GLM-5.2, 而这玩意原始精度要到1.5TB, 本地跑的很少有富到这个程度的, 所以大家都用各种量化版本, 毕竟4bit量化就只要430GB了.

问题这就来了, 由于 GLM-5.2 的 MTP 采用了非常特殊的 DSA (动态稀疏注意力), 导致目前几个推理引擎 (llama.cpp, vLLM, mlx) 都无法支持. 

其中 llama.cpp, mlx 是完全没办法开 MTP, vLLM 只支持FP8精度的.

而SGLang 没事哈, SGLang 架构比较屌上来就支持同一个计算流使用混合精度. 所以直接用 GLM-5.2-W4AFP8 就行. 

所以回到这几个不支持的推理引擎, 大部分的量化版本 GLM-5.2 开了 MTP 反而会掉速度. 甚至有的量化版本直接把MTP部分给砍了(mlx). 

而社区作者dnhkng搞了个缝合方法, 最终搞出了 GLM-5.2-AWQ-INT4-FP8-MTP-delta, 即 底座用 INT4（走 Marlin 算子）+ MTP 用 FP8（保持精度）同时还能让vLLM 支持. 速度从原来的 2 token/s 直接飙升到了 43.39 token/s (绑定NUMA+MTP-3)

所以目前位置 SGLang 和 vLLM (魔改版)都能直接火力全开跑带MTP的 GLM-5.2了. 而 llama.cpp和mlx用户还需要再等等. 社区还在弄.

这个作者的blog (过程极其精彩, 有不少优化技巧): https://t.co/DpJRYMjbYV

#glm52 #mtp #dsa

text:
据 WIRED 报道，在围绕 Fable 5 模型解禁的谈判中，Anthropic 联合创始人 Tom Brown 已经取代 Amodei，成为与特朗普政府对话的主要代表。一位直接了解通话内容的人士说：“Tom Brown 不像 Dario 那样拧巴，他能正常沟通。”

事情的起因要回到 6 月 12 日。当天美国商务部以国家安全为由，对 Anthropic 最新发布的 Fable 5 和 Mythos 5 两款模型发出出口管制令，要求禁止任何外国公民访问，包括 Anthropic 自己的外籍员工。由于无法按国籍筛选用户，Anthropic 被迫对所有用户关闭了这两款模型。

触发这一切的导火索是有公司（据报道是亚马逊的研究团队）声称找到了绕过 Fable 5 安全护栏的方法，可以释放底层 Mythos 模型的网络安全能力。Anthropic 认为这只是一个狭窄的漏洞，不构成全面的越狱，但政府没有被说服。

这是美国政府首次用出口管制手段直接下架一款 AI 模型，影响了数以亿计的用户。Anthropic 其他模型不受影响。

过去几天，白宫和 Anthropic 进行了多轮通话，既有高层对话，也有双方技术团队参与的工作组讨论。核心议题是：Anthropic 需要拿出什么样的证据，才能打消政府对越狱风险的担忧。但这里有个概念层面的难题，独立的网络安全专家越来越倾向于认为，AI 模型的安全护栏从根本上就只是权宜之计，高水平用户和未来的 AI 模型迟早能找到绕过的方法。

白宫态度转暖的直接原因，是 Amodei 不再出现在谈判桌上。知情人士说，Amodei 太难沟通，不听对方的诉求。取而代之的是 Tom Brown 和 Anthropic 公共政策负责人 Sarah Heck。

Tom Brown 是 Anthropic 七位联合创始人之一，MIT 毕业，曾在 OpenAI 担任 GPT-3 的首席工程师，是那篇被引用超过 6 万次的 GPT-3 论文的第一作者。目前在 Anthropic 负责计算基础设施。

Amodei 跟特朗普政府的摩擦不是第一次了。今年 2 月，他拒绝了五角大楼要求删除"禁止将 Claude 用于大规模国内监控和全自主武器"的合同条款，Anthropic 随后被国防部列为供应链风险，联邦机构被要求停用 Claude。3 月底联邦法官发出了临时禁令，认定国防部的行为构成典型的第一修正案报复。

国会也开始介入。上周，两党四名众议员联名致信商务部长 Howard Lutnick，要求解释出口管制的法律依据、技术评估过程、以及恢复模型公开访问的具体标准和时间表。信中还问了一个对整个行业都很关键的问题：其他 AI 公司的前沿模型是否也可能面临类似限制？回复截止日期是 6 月 26 日，也就是后天。商务部尚未表态是否会按时回应。

Fable 5 何时能重新上线，目前没有明确时间表。但接下来几天，Anthropic 需要做什么才能解除管制，可能会变得更清晰。

白宫态度转暖的直接原因，是 Amodei 不再出现在谈判桌上。知情人士说，Amodei 太难沟通，不听对方的诉求。取而代之的是 Tom Brown 和 Anthropic 公共政策负责人 Sarah Heck。

Tom Brown 是 Anthropic 七位联合创始人之一，MIT 毕业，曾在 OpenAI 担任 GPT-3 的首席工程师，是那篇被引用超过 6 万次的 GPT-3 论文的第一作者。目前在 Anthropic 负责计算基础设施。

Amodei 跟特朗普政府的摩擦不是第一次了。今年 2 月，他拒绝了五角大楼要求删除"禁止将 Claude 用于大规模国内监控和全自主武器"的合同条款，Anthropic 随后被国防部列为供应链风险，联邦机构被要求停用 Claude。3 月底联邦法官发出了临时禁令，认定国防部的行为构成典型的第一修正案报复。

国会也开始介入。上周，两党四名众议员联名致信商务部长 Howard Lutnick，要求解释出口管制的法律依据、技术评估过程、以及恢复模型公开访问的具体标准和时间表。信中还问了一个对整个行业都很关键的问题：其他 AI 公司的前沿模型是否也可能面临类似限制？回复截止日期是 6 月 26 日，也就是后天。商务部尚未表态是否会按时回应。

Fable 5 何时能重新上线，目前没有明确时间表。但接下来几天，Anthropic 需要做什么才能解除管制，可能会变得更清晰。

text:
Stock Market Outlook

Valuations for stocks have fallen a bit this year even as prices have risen but some of that is due to one-time factors that probably won’t repeat (mark to market gains on AI stock holdings). Stocks are still expensive and we are probably getting close to a cyclical peak in tech earnings. Given the changes to the sector, it may be a secular peak but there’s no way to know yet. 

At the same time, interest rates are rising which is generally a headwind for higher stock prices but inflation expectations have been falling as the Iran War winds down (assuming it really is). Sentiment is too strange to parse right now; there’s speculative activity all over the place but more traditional sentiment metrics are pretty neutral. 

I’d suggest approaching the second half with low expectations and a sense of history. Midterm election years – second years of the Presidential cycle – are historically the worst of the four year cycle but tend to perform better after the election. Having already exceeded the historical average for this year, a more subdued second half would not surprise me.

That’s just a few of many unknowns right now and there are more, some of which we can’t even imagine right now.  As with past technological changes I suspect it will not be the tech companies who build the AI infrastructure that will be the biggest beneficiaries. The companies that built the railroads in the 19th century weren’t the biggest beneficiaries; indeed many of them went bankrupt. 

But Sears created an entire industry on mail order delivered on cheap rails. It wasn’t the companies that laid all that fiber optic cable around the turn of the century who benefitted either. Global Crossing went bankrupt installing fiber no one knew what to do with but Amazon and the streaming companies turned that capacity into cash. 

And I expect AI to be no different. If computing power becomes ubiquitous and cheap – and I think that is highly likely – it will be the companies that put that excess capacity to its best use that benefit the most. That may include some technology companies – ironically considering how the market is punishing them today, I think software companies are an obvious beneficiary – but most of them will be from other sectors.

Can tech stocks keep outperforming? I suppose anything is possible. The sector has, after all, been outperforming for ten years and continues to do so while still posting great earnings. But an AI-dominated technology sector isn’t the same technology sector that beat the rest of the market by 15%/year for ten years. 

All good things come to an end and technology’s run will too. The industry has already invested over a trillion dollars in AI since 2023 and the run rate is expected to be over $1 trillion a year by 2030. Or so some analyst guessed in a “research” report I read recently. Jensen Huang, who might be talking his book, says the total of the physical infrastructure installed on the global grid will reach $3 to $4 trillion by the turn of the decade. Can the industry turn all this investment into a return that justifies today’s stock prices? They better.

text:
Wild Cards, Second Acts, and a 71-Year-Old Guy Who Still Can’t Sing

Last weekend, 57-year-old Chuck did something because 13-year-old Chuck would’ve wanted it that way.

I flew to Detroit, ate an absurdly good Detroit-style pizza right off Eight Mile Road, then drove to Battle Creek to watch David Lee Roth at a casino. The man is 71. The voice is shot, he’s making up the lyrics as he goes, and he was objectively terrible.

But damn… it was glorious in all its wonder. I loved every minute of it.

I brought our head of data security, Sam Texas, with me. The deal was that when we weren’t eating pizza or watching Diamond Dave embarrass himself, he had to teach me how to code. So we built a ridiculous blackjack game — my face is on every card, the dealer talks shit like Dennis Miller, and we threw in wild cards just to watch what happens. I’ve now officially told Collin I’m part of the engineering department.

But not everything has been fun and games.  Here’s the part I don’t usually say out loud.

We’ve done some legitimately insane things to keep Collide alive — like throwing a 400-person crawfish boil in my own front yard just to scrape together enough money for payroll.  Equally crazy, every share I own, I paid for myself. That’s what it took to get us here.

Thankfully, those days are behind us. Today we’re a software company backed by Mercury Fund, which means we’re raising capital every twelve months — typical for a startup at our stage. But it’s sure as hell better than selling crawfish boils.

Right now I’m not taking a salary. Over the last six years, I’ve drawn basically nothing so we can allocate capital where it matters most. I don’t need the money — I’ve already had that part of my life. What I need now is a second act. Not just to prove to myself — but if I’m being honest, to everyone else too — that the initial one wasn’t an accident.

That first time around I was the weird hoodie guy in private equity. I never took myself seriously, but I took what I did very seriously. What hurt most was that a handful of people I thought supported me — people I genuinely respected — would smile to my face and then talk shit about me behind my back.
There were definitely days I believed the criticism — days I genuinely wondered if I should just conform. Hell, I did own an Armani suit and a couple of Hermès ties — and I could have bought more.

But even with all that self-doubt, something in me still believed that just being me might actually be enough.

Now I’m trying to do it again — this time building something from scratch, learning to code at 57, and betting the whole thing on building AI to completely revolutionize how the energy industry works.

Watching a 71-year-old David Lee Roth still out there giving everything he’s got — even with an empty tank — hit me harder than I expected. Because some days this journey feels exactly like that.

I don’t know how this story ends. But for the first time in a long time, I’m more optimistic than I’ve ever been.

And by the way… that 71-year-old man with no voice still commanded the stage, brought the house down, had the crowd eating out of his hand, and walked off to a standing ovation.

I think 57-year-old Chuck was every bit as delighted as 13-year-old Chuck would’ve been.

Sip slowly, my friends.

@DavidLeeRoth @heysamtexas

Meditation is completely subjective and can’t be measured.

That’s a limiting belief.

At Dojo, we analyzed qualified meditation sessions with second-by-second heart-rate data.

What we found:

76.8% of sessions lowered heart rate
Avg drop: 6.5 BPM
Avg time to lowest HR: 7.6 min

Heart rate is not a “score” for meditation.
But meditation doesn’t have to stay a black box.

Subjective experience matters.
Physiological response matters too.

Press release + full study link in first comment.

text:
I have discussed this very question in a 2023 essay I published in Sam Harris: Critical Responses. Short answer: You can’t. Excerpt below.

"In addition to consciousness, humans (and presumably some other animals) have a faculty of reason. We all have some intuitive sense of what reason is, but what is it in general terms? [Sam] Harris’s preferred philosopher for defining consciousness, Thomas Nagel, explains in his 1997 book, The Last Word: “The idea of reason . . . refers to nonlocal and nonrelative methods of justification—methods that distinguish universally legitimate from illegitimate inferences and that aim at reaching the truth in a nonrelative sense” (The Last Word, p. 5).

Reason cannot be an illusion, either. To see why, let’s consider a prime example of reason: rules of logic.

A basic rule of logic that we can all grasp is: ‘If P then Q’ plus ‘P’ implies ‘Q’, where ‘P’ and ‘Q’ are one among an infinitude of possible statements about the world. We also grasp that this rule of logic—fancily called ‘Modus Ponens’ by philosophers—cannot fail to be valid under any circumstance. By ‘valid’ I mean that it is impossible for the premises—’If P then Q’ and ‘P’—to be true and the conclusion— ’Q’—to nevertheless be false; it is impossible that ‘If P then Q’ plus ‘P’ implies ‘not-Q’. So we grasp that the rule of logic is valid always, everywhere, and for everyone—it is universally valid. At least, as long as we understand the meanings of the words ‘plus’, ‘if’, ‘then’, and ‘implies’ in their normal senses.

Imagine now that some radical skeptic comes along and argues:

Maybe the rule of logic—’If P then Q’ plus ‘P’ implies ‘Q’—only seems universally valid to you, but it really isn’t. It might only seem that way to you because something you are unaware of—an evil demon scrambling your brains, or invisible aliens beaming thoughts into your head, or God divinely planting beliefs into your mind, or some genetic mutation in one of your ancestors millions of years ago—is deluding you into thinking it’s universally valid. You can’t rule out this possibility, so you can’t be sure that that rule of logic, which seems universally valid to you, really is universally valid.

This is tantamount to suggesting that the universal validity of the rule of logic might be an illusion. But this makes no sense, for a couple of reasons.

First, the argument of the radical skeptic gives us no positive understanding of how the rule of logic, whose invalidity we cannot imagine, might after all fail to be valid. When we look back at the rule of logic, after listening to the skeptic’s argument, we still cannot help but think that it is universally valid. This is unlike, say, the skeptical hypothesis that you are a brain-in-a-vat and an evil scientist is manipulating your brain to create false beliefs, such as believing that you have hands—here you do get a positive understanding of how your belief that you have hands, which is hard for you to imagine the falsity of, could be false after all.

Second, the radical skeptic’s argument actually has the
form of the rule of logic that it is trying to cast doubt upon. In other words it presupposes the universal validity of the rule of logic. The argument asserts, ‘If you can’t rule out the possibility that something you are unaware of is deluding you into thinking that the rule of logic is universally valid, then you can’t be sure that the rule of logic, which seems universally valid to you, really is universally valid.’ Call this ‘If P then Q’. It also says that ‘You can’t rule out the possibility that something you are unaware of is deluding you into thinking that the rule of logic is universally valid’. Call this ‘P’. So the argument has the form, ‘If P then Q’ plus ‘P’ implies ‘Q’. If the radical skeptic’s argument were valid, it would apply to itself and therefore refute itself. And if the argument is not valid, then it doesn’t establish the possibility that the rule of logic is an illusion…

This is exactly why GLM, a mere 750B model, can compete with 2T-level frontier models.

text:
There's a particular way smart people blow themselves up, and it looks like winning right up until it doesn't.
 
You build a huge position in something. You're right, and you keep getting more right, so you add. And you never take any profit. You average up and up and up, and because everyone can see your position, the whole market knows exactly where your pain is.
 
You can be right for a very long time doing this. That's the trap. The longer it works, the more convinced you get, the bigger and more visible the position becomes, and the less staying power you have left if it ever turns.
 
Then one day the market turns to you and says, you can't add any more, you're out of fresh money, and the thing you own is a long way underwater. What now? And there's no answer, because you never built any room to be wrong.
 
For me, the lesson is that taking some profit on the way up isn't weakness, it's what keeps you in the game. You could have banked a chunk, locked in a fortune, kept your staying power. Instead you keep averaging up until the market turns round and asks what you're going to do about it, and there's no answer. 

Options make this scenario avoidable. those who don't listen will learn the expensive way.

I came across this chart from @socialcapital recently and found it surprisingly thought-provoking.

The obvious takeaway is that most people's wealth is tied up in their home.

The less obvious takeaway is what happens as you move up the wealth ladder.

Home equity gradually becomes less important, while business equity becomes increasingly important.

Around the same time, I read @paulg's recent essay on how people make billion-dollar fortunes. His argument was that the biggest fortunes tend to come from owning a meaningful piece of something that grows exponentially.

That reminded me of something @sama has written about before: technology is one of the few places where a small group of people can create an enormous amount of value in a relatively short period of time.

Different people. Different eras. Different arguments.

Yet they all seem to be describing the same phenomenon from different angles.

Ownership of fast-growing assets matters disproportionately.

Which makes me wonder whether this is partly what's driving so much of the recent discussion around a "permanent underclass."

If most people build wealth through housing, while the largest fortunes are increasingly created through ownership of rapidly growing businesses, then the gap between those two paths may matter more than we realize.

Viewed through that lens, @ycombinator's core idea feels almost obvious: build something people want, own a piece of it, and let compounding do the rest.

Maybe that's why, despite all the discussion around housing affordability, inequality, and a permanent underclass, some people remain stubbornly bullish on building.

result.text:
I came across this chart from @socialcapital recently and found it surprisingly thought-provoking.

The obvious takeaway is that most people's wealth is tied up in their home.

The less obvious takeaway is what happens as you move up the wealth ladder.

Home equity gradually becomes less important, while business equity becomes increasingly important.

Around the same time, I read @paulg's recent essay on how people make billion-dollar fortunes. His argument was that the biggest fortunes tend to come from owning a meaningful piece of something that grows exponentially.

That reminded me of something @sama has written about before: technology is one of the few places where a small group of people can create an enormous amount of value in a relatively short period of time.

Different people. Different eras. Different arguments.

Yet they all seem to be describing the same phenomenon from different angles.

Ownership of fast-growing assets matters disproportionately.

Which makes me wonder whether this is partly what's driving so much of the recent discussion around a "permanent underclass."

If most people build wealth through housing, while the largest fortunes are increasingly created through ownership of rapidly growing businesses, then the gap between those two paths may matter more than we realize.

Viewed through that lens, @ycombinator's core idea feels almost obvious: build something people want, own a piece of it, and let compounding do the rest.

Maybe that's why, despite all the discussion around housing affordability, inequality, and a permanent underclass, some people remain stubbornly bullish on building.

Among the most iconic Derek Jeter jerseys to ever surface, this one has it all.

He wore this jersey.

Beyond its connection to that legendary moment, the jersey was also conclusively photo matched across a span of 71 games during the 2004 season and post season, making it one of the most extensively used Jeter jerseys to surface. Additionally, this jersey was photographed to ten baseball cards and four covers of Sporting News. This is a true cornerstone piece representing Derek Jeter, “The Captain,“ combining extensive use, and one of the most iconic plays of the modern era.

SIA is proud to help document and authenticate such an iconic piece of sports history.

Wrote up something fun I’ve been poking at: when LLM agents repeatedly rewrite their own experiences into textual “lessons,” their memory can get worse, not better.

Across several environments, we found a recurring pattern: forced consolidation often degrades useful experience into faulty or overgeneralized memories. 
Interestingly, models seem much better at managing examples as memory objects than at distilling them into reusable routines.

Maybe we should be more careful about asking agents to constantly “consolidate” experience into lessons 🤔?

I’m new to this area, so I’d love thoughts. I may be missing context or just wrong on parts of it — please don’t hesitate to let me know! Discussions are always welcome.

We’ve been working on something new: OpenTag 🔥 open-source @ agent mentions for GitHub, Slack, and beyond.
If the idea resonates with you, a ⭐ would mean a lot:
https://t.co/NGK81KZq86

The idea is simple: AI agents should be able to join the work where it already happens.

Instead of copying a GitHub issue, PR, or Slack discussion into another chat window, you should be able to tag an agent directly in the thread, let it work with the right tools and context, and get progress, results, changed files, or even a PR back in the same place.

We built OpenTag around an open, auditable dispatch layer: a mention becomes a normalized event, routed only to an explicitly bound local runner.

This is more than parsing an @ mention. We’re thinking about repo bindings, local execution, isolated branches, callbacks, leases, audit history, and making different agent runtimes interchangeable without hiding what’s happening behind a black box.

OpenTag is still an early v0, but we’re sharing it now because we want the direction to be shaped in the open.

If you want to help make “tag an agent into the work” an open protocol rather than a closed feature, we’d love your feedback.
